{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''Neil A. Chriss''' is a [[mathematician]], [[Academic staff|academic]], [[hedge fund]] manager,<ref>Imogen Rose-Smith, (July 20, 2011) [http://www.institutionalinvestor.com/Article/2867611/Search/Neil-Chrisss-Multistrat-Hedge-Fund-Puts-Up-The-Numbers.html?Keywords=%22Neil+Chriss%22 "Neil Chriss's Multistrat Hedge Fund Puts Up The Numbers"]. ''[[Institutional Investor (magazine)|Institutional Investor]]''.</ref> [[philanthropist]] and a founding board member of the charity organization "[[Math for America]]" which seeks to improve math education in the [[United States]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.mathforamerica.org/web/guest/about-us/board/neil-chriss |title=Neil Chriss biography at "Math for America" webpage |access-date=2011-11-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120407063227/http://www.mathforamerica.org/web/guest/about-us/board/neil-chriss |archive-date=2012-04-07 |url-status=dead }}</ref>  Chriss also serves on the board of trustees of the [[Institute for Advanced Study]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ias.edu/news/press-releases/2011/12/19/chriss |title=Institute for Advanced Study Appoints Neil Chriss to Board of Trustees |access-date=2012-01-06 |archive-date=2012-01-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120121113726/http://www.ias.edu/news/press-releases/2011/12/19/chriss |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Early career==
Chriss learned programming at the age of 11. He developed a videogame called D' Fuse and sold it to Tymac when he was a sophomore in high school. The game quickly faded when the Commodore 64 with 64K of memory and much better graphics appeared.<ref>R. Lindsay and Barry Schachter, "How I became a Quant", Wiley (2007), {{ISBN|978-0-470-05062-0}}</ref>

Chriss went to the [[University of Chicago]], where he majored in mathematics. Following his junior year in college, he worked at [[Fermilab]] with Myron Campbell and Bruce Denby; he developed a neural network to find [[Bottom quark|b-quark]] jets.<ref>Denby, Cambell, Bedeschi, Chriss, et al.,, "Neural Networks for Triggering," IEEE Tians. Nucl. Sci, 37(2) (1990), 248–254</ref> He then earned his master's degree in [[applied mathematics]] at [[Caltech]].<ref name="hmc.edu">{{cite web |url=http://www.hmc.edu/about1/governance/boardoftrustees1/board-of-trustee-biographies.html |title=Board of Trustee Biographies |accessdate=2012-01-08 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://archive.today/20120801093220/http://www.hmc.edu/about1/governance/boardoftrustees1/board-of-trustee-biographies.html |archivedate=2012-08-01 }}</ref>

Chriss studied [[pure mathematics]] at the [[University of Chicago]], working in the [[Langlands program|Langlands Program]]. He received a Ph.D. in 1993, with the thesis ''A Geometric Construction of the Iwahori-Hecke Algebra''.<ref>The thesis followed up on [[David Kazhdan]]  and [[George Lusztig]], "Proof of the Deligne-Langlands conjecture for Hecke algebras", Invent. Math, 87 (1987), 153–215</ref> With [[Victor Ginzburg]], he wrote a book on [[algebraic geometry]] and [[representation theory]].<ref>Victor Ginzburg and Neil Chriss. ''Representation Theory and Complex Geometry''. Birkhäuser, 1997.</ref>

==Academia==
Chriss's first academic job (1993–1994) was at the [[University of Toronto]], where he wrote "Representation Theory and Complex Geometry" with Ginzburg.  At Toronto, [[John M. Liew]] introduced Chriss to "[[Quantitative analyst|quant]]" finance, [[probability theory]], [[stochastic calculus]] and [[Black–Scholes]] option pricing theory.

At the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in 1994–1995, Chriss began the book "Black–Scholes and Beyond: Option Pricing Models" (Irwin, 1996). In 1995, he was hired for the summer in the Quantitative Strategies group of [[Emanuel Derman]] at [[Goldman Sachs]]. In 1994, Derman and Kani published a paper<ref>I.Kani and E.Derman, "Riding on a Smile", ''[[Risk (magazine)|Risk]]'' '''7'''(2) (1994), pp. 32–39</ref> that showed how to fit a [[Binomial options pricing model|binomial tree]] to price all options trading in the market at that time. Chriss helped  extend their work from binomial to [[trinomial tree]]s.<ref>E. Derman, I. Kani, N. Chriss, "Implied trinomial trees of the volatility smile", ''Journal of Derivatives'' (1996)</ref>

Chriss received a grant from NSF and went to [[Harvard University]] Mathematics Department in 1996. Despite the offer of an assistant professorship at Harvard in 1997, he moved to Wall Street.

==Wall Street==
Risk Magazine named Chriss one of the "Top Ten to Watch in the next Ten Years" in 1997.<ref>{{Cite news|title= Exclusive: How Hutchin Hill Took Down JPMorgan|author= Jacob Wolinsky |publisher= Value Walk |date = July 9, 2012}}</ref>

In 1997, Chriss joined the quant research group in [[Morgan Stanley]] to work on portfolio trading for their cash equities operational dealing desk. He wrote a paper "Optimal execution of portfolio transactions" with [[Robert Almgren]].<ref>R.Almgren and N.Chriss, "Optimal execution of portfolio transactions" J. Risk, 3 (Winter 2000/2001) pp.5–39</ref> The Institutional Investor<ref>[http://www.institutionalinvestor.com The Institutional Investor] magazine</ref> published an article about Algorithmic Trading in its November 2004 issue, titled "The Orders Battle", which noted that Chriss's paper "helped lay the groundwork for arrival-price algorithms being developed on Wall Street." The work has been widely cited since.<ref>David Leinweber, "Algo vs. Algo", The Institutional Investor's Alpha, February 2007</ref><ref>A TRADE Guide to Broker Algorithms, The TRADE, Issue 3, Jan–Mar 2005</ref> Chriss also wrote articles on the following topics: "Competitive bids for principal program trades",<ref>Robert Almgren and Neil Chriss, "Bidding principles" ''Risk'', June 2003</ref> "Value under liquidation".<ref>Robert Almgren and Neil Chriss, "Value under liquidation", ''Risk'', Dec. 1999</ref> At Morgan Stanley, Peter Muller inspired Chriss to pursue quantitative trading.

In 1998, Chriss moved into [[Investment management|portfolio management]], joining the Goldman Sachs Asset Management (GSAM) Quantitative Strategies group to develop a new trading strategy, after Cliff Asness, [[John M. Liew]] and Bob Krail left to form [[AQR Capital Management]].

In 2000, Chriss left Goldman Sachs to found ICor Brokerage Inc., a derivatives trading firm.<ref name="hmc.edu"/> In 2001, ICor joined forces with  [[Reuters]], forming a joint venture, ICor Brokerage Ltd.<ref name="ICorReutersMerger">{{cite web | url= http://www.finextra.com/fullstory.asp?id=3008 | title= Reuters and ICor combine for electronic derivatives | publisher = Finextra Research | accessdate= 2008-06-30}}</ref>  Reuters bought out ICor in 2004.<ref name="ICorReutersBuyout">{{cite web | url= http://www.finextra.com/fullstory.asp?id=11438 | title= Reuters assumes full control of ICor Brokerage; targets interest rate swaps | publisher = Finextra Research | accessdate= 2008-06-30}}</ref>

==Mathematical finance education==
Chriss was asked by [[New York University]] [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences]] to be the first (part-time) director of the Program in Mathematics in Finance.<ref>[http://www.math.nyu.edu/financial_mathematics/ NYU Program in Mathematics in Finance]</ref> At Courant from 1997 to 2003, Chriss recruited [[Jim Gatheral]], Steve Allen, Peter Fraenkel (now head of Quantitative IT at [[UBS]]) and [[Nassim Taleb]].

In 2003 Chriss became executive director of the University of Chicago Financial Mathematics Program.

==Hedge funds==
In 2003, Chriss joined the Stamford, Connecticut hedge fund [[SAC Capital]], working there until early 2007.

Chriss then founded the hedge fund "Hutchin Hill Capital". [[Renaissance Technologies]]' Meritage Fund provided $300 million of capital to Hutchin Hill.{{Citation needed|date=June 2011}}

==Recent research==
With R. Almgren, Chriss wrote a paper on optimizing a portfolio.<ref>Robert Almgren and Neil Chriss, "Optimal portfolios from ordering information", ''Journal of Risk'', Fall 2006</ref> They submitted a [http://www.freshpatents.com/Method-and-system-for-portfolio-optimization-from-ordering-information-dt20060824ptan20060190371.php patent application] on the method.

[[Nigel Goldenfeld]], a professor of physics at [[University of Illinois]], recommends Chriss's book ''Black–Scholes and Beyond'' to those of his students "contemplating a career in quantitative finance", as giving an "Excellent overview of modern day finance, financial models, and their shortcomings.  A great blend of practical and theoretical knowledge, clearly presented".<ref name="ProfGoldenfeld">{{cite web | url=http://guava.physics.uiuc.edu/~nigel/finance.html | title=Job Hunting on Wall Street | publisher=University of Illinois | work=Finance for Physicists | date=March 2009 | accessdate=December 9, 2011 | author=Goldenfeld, Nigel}}</ref>
